topic: Route planning and altitude selection (Skyway Code)
summary: Plan a VFR route with a pilot's log (PLOG), error-check it, and back it up with a plotted chart. Choose a safety altitude by adding 500 or 1,000 ft to the Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF) and study at least 5 NM either side of track. Avoid whole-number cruising altitudes, plan descents at 3 NM per 1,000 ft, use Take 2 near controlled airspace and plan a transit about 10 minutes ahead. Built from the Skyway Code pp.41-45.
src: The Skyway Code (CAP 1535 v4, Nov 2023), pp.41-45
sections: The PLOG
A pilot's log holds headings, distances and times for each leg, frequencies, planned and safety altitudes and the fuel plan
Gross-error check all figures, for example confusing 030° with 300°, and keep winds aloft up to date
Plot the route on a paper chart too: it is the backup if the moving map device fails
Pick a radio frequency for each stage, consider UK FIS, and note hazards: aerodromes, danger areas, parachuting, glider sites and cable launches
Many busy GA aerodromes have no ATZ. VFR traffic may bunch near visual reference points (VRPs) and beacons
Maximum Elevation Figure and safety altitude
The MEF is the large figure in each lat/long box on the VFR chart. It is the higher of the highest obstacle or the highest terrain plus 300 ft
Obstacles under 300 ft AGL may not be in the data, hence the 300 ft. Obstacles over 300 ft are captured with no extra margin
Study the area at least 5 NM either side of track
No legal safety altitude exists for VFR but add 500 ft or 1,000 ft over the highest obstacle or terrain
Set safety altitudes below which you will not descend without reversing course or diverting
If IFR-qualified, consider planning the flight as IFR from the outset
Choosing a cruising altitude
Avoid whole-number altitudes such as 3,000 ft. Pick random ones such as 4,200 ft or 5,400 ft
Flying higher can give a better view, greater glide range, lower traffic density, less turbulence, better TAS and fuel burn, and better radio reception
SERA VFR cruising levels apply above 3,000 ft AGL (starting at FL35) but are not mandatory in the UK. In some European states they are mandatory
Descent planning rule: 3 NM for every 1,000 ft, so about 30 NM from 10,000 ft. Ground speed x 5 gives the descent rate in ft/min (100 kt is about 500 ft/min, a 3° path)
Avoiding infringements
Study controlled airspace boundaries: vertical limits change over short distances
Mark a route that clearly avoids CAS rather than navigating around edges ad hoc
Take 2: keep 2 NM or 200 ft from CAS, Danger and Restricted areas, ATZs and similar
Request a UK FIS near CAS, or use a Frequency Monitoring Code
Use the relevant aerodrome QNH, not the RPS. Do not use IFR waypoints for VFR navigation. Make user waypoints at recognisable features
In local handling, set altitudes you must not exceed and include 'airspace' in HASELL checks
Planning a transit of CAS
Have a plan B. For CTRs check for preferred VFR routes in the aerodrome AIP entry (AD 2.22)
Request about 10 minutes before the boundary and calculate an ETA at the boundary
Crossing overhead at right angles to the main runway can avoid aerodrome traffic
Be ready for a different route or altitude. Overflying with vertical clearance is an effective avoidance

o: Higher of the highest obstacle or highest terrain plus 300 ft
The average terrain height in the box, rounded up to 100 ft
A safe cruising altitude for the whole of the box
The highest obstacle in the box plus 1,000 ft, rounded up
